railway-regrade.text: The railway runs on a graded formation: the turning loop level with the station and the main line climbing 1 in 40 from the junction, in rock cuttings and on embankments. A post-pack step regrades the terrain inside the line's earthworks only and clears their trees, and every tree within 10 m of the open line, so that no crown the renderer grows comes within a metre of a coach's side.

basis.choice: railway_profile: regrade

basis.quote: probably more trees, or a spur of hillside

basis.note: the existing heightfield put the junction 36 m above the station 68 m away and the foot of the loop 25 m below it

railway-tunnel.text: The main line enters a tunnel 180 m up it from the turnout's toe, at the first point where the hillside stands a headwall and a 2 m margin over the formation across the portal's width. Before it the line climbs 1 in 40 on an embankment up to 2 m high, across a dry valley made up where the train's screen closes it, then in a rock cutting up to 13 m deep. The hill stands for the spur that hides the departing train, which leaves heading as White Hound's line arrives: from the north, or slightly west of north.

basis.quote: which prevents the train from being seen from the station once it has rounded the bend
On my re-worked, canon-consistent map it's coming from the north, or slightly west of north.

basis.choice: railway_profile: regrade

railway-culvert.text: Where the cutting round the foot of the loop meets the burn beside it, the burn's water gives way to the earthworks; no other water is touched.

basis.choice: railway_profile: regrade

basis.quote: You can change the water layers, that's fine.

basis.note: the burn runs 10 m from the loop's centreline there, about 10 m above the formation on the cutting's side; 2 texels (8 m²) of it are dried

railway-curves.text: No curve is tighter than about 3 chains (60 m; the tightest is 61 m), which a tender engine can take at walking pace. White Hound's ink kinks to about 40 m round his drawing of the engine, so the line there is designed: the engine stands on the curve round the foot of the loop (radius 66 m, the drawn foot's own) with both ends on its registered segment, the gentlest S joins it to the coaches' straight, and the foot rejoins his drawn east side.

basis.quote: if the loop is plausibly tight, there's nothing that says the train can't go slow, right? I'll leave that up to you.

basis.note: the loop is drawn up to 6 m away from the built line where it swings round the drawn engine, and within 2.4 m elsewhere

lamplit-windows.text: Lit windows glow with lamplight, not white: candlelight (about 2200 K) in the castle, the coaches' lamps (about 2700 K) and dimmer oil lamps (about 2400 K) at the station. Some rooms are lit only dimly, the glow stays short of the tone curve's white shoulder at the night exposure, and lit windows shine in the lake.

basis.quote: what's the realistic color for Windows at Dusk? Is there anything more you could do about it?
because the station has lighted windows even when the platform itself is dark

station-terrace.text: The station stands on a level terrace from the track to the boundary wall along the platform: the spur that rose up to 20 m over its north-west half is cut back and the ground that fell 3-6 m below its south-east half is made up, so the platform, its back wall, the road outside and the building share one level. The lake path leaves through the gap between the wall's two ends in a short cutting through the spur.

basis.quote: a narrow door which lets onto the road outside
a way through this barrier, which leads to an entrance in the Hogwarts boundary wall

basis.choice: railway_profile: regrade

village-detail-where-seen.text: Every footprint is built, and the village keeps to its share of the payload by spending fine detail where the flyover sees it: chimney stacks are capped flush in pale stone rather than under overhanging copes, a raised door's steps are one stone block, and off the High Street a stack carries one pot, a back wall one window and a storey-and-a-half front one dormer. The camera passes 50 m and more above the village, where a cope's overhang or a step's riser spans a pixel or two.

basis.note: built with all its detail the village came to 225k triangles, about 1.6 MB of payload at 8 bytes a triangle, over the 1.5 MB it may add before its named buildings; trimmed, 174k

village-levels.text: The village's building records also give two coarser levels of detail and a shadow caster, so whatever places a building places it at every level. lod1 lays every window and door flat on its wall, stands the chimney stacks in the roofs as boxes and fills each roof's skin in, trimmed back to its gables so their windows show; it keeps base courses, dormers, the named buildings' bays, buttresses and roof features and the kirkyard's and gardens' walls, but no fittings, painted margins or reveals. lod2 is each building's walls under its filled-in skin, which keeps the eaves that the flyover sees from above; the shadow caster, which the page draws again only when the sun moves, is its walls and attic, the cheapest, with what stands out beyond the eaves and casts a shadow of its own: Gladrags' blind and the Shack's fence as built, the kirkyard's wall, and each garden's wall and gate as one slab along them. Seen from above it leaves no patch of more than a square metre of the full village farther than 0.75 m from it. They are designed for frame time, none cut to fit the payload's room. The payload carries each level that passes its guards and saves enough triangles, and the page chooses among them for each view.

basis.note: approved plan: levels of detail and the triangle budget are among the village's design categories
live frame time ranks above page load

at site X, of the full village's 171k triangles lod1 takes 68k, lod2 32k and the shadow caster 21k; packed alone, they take 0.64, 0.31 and 0.23 MB. Without its eaves lod2 would take about 21k, but its roofs seen from above would cover a sixth less (intersection over union 0.84)

integration found that the walls and attic alone cast no shadow for the kirkyard's wall, the blind or the fence: seen from above, they left the kirkyard's wall (56 m²), the blind (9 m²), the fence (4.5 m²) and the gardens' walls (up to 3.6 m² each) farther than 0.75 m from the caster; with them, no patch of more than 0.3 m²
